subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which term describes all the organisms of one species living in a particular area at one time?
questions.explain: A population is all the members of a single species living together in the same area at the same time.

questions.q: What is the correct term for the place where an organism lives?
questions.explain: A habitat is the specific place or environment in which an organism lives.

questions.q: Which term best describes all the populations of different species living together in the same area, plus their non-living surroundings?
questions.explain: An ecosystem includes the community of organisms together with the non-living (abiotic) components of their environment.

questions.q: Which piece of apparatus is used to estimate the abundance of plants in a habitat?
questions.explain: A quadrat is a square frame placed on the ground to sample and estimate the abundance of slow-moving or non-moving organisms such as plants.

questions.q: Why should quadrats be placed at random positions when estimating the number of plants in a field?
options: To make counting the plants faster
To avoid bias so the sample represents the whole area
To ensure every quadrat contains the same species
To reduce the number of quadrats needed
questions.explain: Random placement prevents the investigator from biasing the sample, giving a result more representative of the whole habitat.

questions.q: A student uses a 0.25 m² quadrat and finds a mean of 3 dandelions per quadrat. Estimate the number of dandelions in a field of 100 m².
questions.explain: Density is 3 per 0.25 m² = 12 per m², so 12 x 100 m² gives an estimated 1200 dandelions.

questions.q: In a food chain, what name is given to organisms such as green plants that make their own food by photosynthesis?
questions.explain: Producers are organisms, typically green plants, that synthesise their own food and form the start of a food chain.

questions.q: What term describes an organism that feeds on dead material and releases nutrients back into the environment?
questions.explain: Decomposers, such as bacteria and fungi, break down dead organisms and waste, recycling nutrients into the ecosystem.

questions.q: In the food chain grass to rabbit to fox, what trophic level does the fox occupy?
questions.explain: Grass is the first level (producer), the rabbit the second (primary consumer), and the fox the third (secondary consumer).

questions.q: Approximately what percentage of energy is typically transferred from one trophic level to the next in a food chain?
questions.explain: Only about 10% of energy is passed on, the rest being lost through respiration, movement, heat and undigested waste.

questions.q: Why do food chains rarely contain more than four or five trophic levels?
options: Predators cannot find enough prey to eat
Energy is lost at each level, leaving too little to support higher levels
There are not enough species on Earth
questions.explain: Because roughly 90% of energy is lost at each transfer, insufficient energy remains to support many further trophic levels.

questions.q: A pyramid of numbers for the food chain oak tree to caterpillar to bird is inverted (bottom bar narrow). What best explains this?
options: The oak tree has less biomass than the birds
One large producer supports many small primary consumers
questions.explain: A single large oak supports many caterpillars, so counting individuals gives a narrow producer bar and an inverted pyramid of numbers.

questions.q: In the carbon cycle, which process removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere?
questions.explain: Photosynthesis by producers takes carbon dioxide out of the air and fixes the carbon into organic compounds.

questions.q: Which two processes return carbon dioxide to the atmosphere in the carbon cycle?
questions.explain: Respiration by living organisms and the combustion (burning) of fuels both release carbon dioxide back into the atmosphere.

questions.q: Which type of bacteria convert nitrogen gas from the air into nitrogen-containing compounds in the soil?
questions.explain: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria, some found in the root nodules of legumes, convert atmospheric nitrogen into usable nitrogen compounds.

questions.q: What is the role of nitrifying bacteria in the nitrogen cycle?
options: They convert nitrates into nitrogen gas
They convert ammonium compounds into nitrates
They convert nitrogen gas into ammonia
They break down proteins into amino acids
questions.explain: Nitrifying bacteria oxidise ammonium compounds into nitrites and then nitrates, which plants can absorb.

questions.q: Which process is carried out by denitrifying bacteria?
options: Converting nitrates in the soil back into nitrogen gas
questions.explain: Denitrifying bacteria break down nitrates, releasing nitrogen gas back into the atmosphere and reducing soil fertility.

questions.q: Excess nitrate fertiliser washing into a lake can cause eutrophication. What is the first main effect of the extra nitrates?
options: Fish immediately die from the nitrates
questions.explain: The extra nitrates cause algae to grow rapidly, forming a bloom that later blocks light and triggers oxygen depletion.

questions.q: In a eutrophic lake, why do fish and other aquatic animals eventually die?
options: Decomposing bacteria use up the dissolved oxygen
Nitrates are toxic to their gills
questions.explain: When algae and plants die, aerobic bacteria decompose them and consume the dissolved oxygen, so animals suffocate.

questions.q: Which pair of gases are the main greenhouse gases contributing to global warming?
questions.explain: Carbon dioxide and methane are the principal greenhouse gases that trap heat and contribute to global warming.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Biology (4BI1) specification; Ecology & the Environment
